lessons.title: Plant tissues, organs and systems
lessons.summary: Explore the tissues of a leaf, how xylem and phloem transport water and sugars, and what controls the rate of transpiration.
objectives: I can name the tissues in a leaf and explain how each is adapted to its function.
I can describe the structure and function of xylem and phloem.
I can explain transpiration and translocation.
I can describe how stomata and guard cells control gas exchange and water loss.
I can explain how light, temperature, humidity and air movement affect the rate of transpiration.

activities.title: The leaf: an organ built from tissues
activities.content:
## Tissues of the leaf

A leaf is a plant **organ** whose main job is photosynthesis. Cut a leaf in cross-section and you find several **tissues**, each adapted to its role:

| Tissue | Where | Adaptation and function |
|---|---|---|
| **Upper epidermis** | Top surface | Thin, transparent layer that lets light through; covered by a **waxy cuticle** that reduces water loss |
| **Palisade mesophyll** | Just under the upper epidermis | Tall, tightly packed cells crammed with **chloroplasts** for maximum photosynthesis |
| **Spongy mesophyll** | Middle of the leaf | Loosely packed cells with **air spaces** so gases can diffuse to and from cells |
| **Xylem and phloem** | In the veins | Transport water and minerals (xylem) and sugars (phloem) |
| **Lower epidermis** | Bottom surface | Contains **stomata**, tiny pores that allow gas exchange |

The leaf is broad and thin, giving a large surface area for absorbing light and a short distance for gases to diffuse.

Plant organs (roots, stems, leaves) are grouped into **organ systems**. The roots, stem and leaves together form the plant's **transport system**, moving water, minerals and sugars between where they are absorbed or made and where they are needed.

question.text: Match each leaf tissue to its adaptation.
question.hint: Think about light at the top, gases in the middle and pores underneath.
question.explanation: The upper epidermis is transparent with a waxy cuticle; palisade cells hold many chloroplasts; spongy mesophyll has air spaces; the lower epidermis holds the stomata.

activities.title: Xylem and phloem
activities.content:
## Two transport tissues

### Xylem

**Xylem** carries **water and dissolved mineral ions** from the roots up to the stem and leaves. This flow is in **one direction only**: upwards.

- Xylem is made of dead cells joined end to end with the end walls removed, forming hollow tubes.
- The walls are strengthened with **lignin**, which makes them waterproof and stops them collapsing, and also helps support the plant.

The movement of water from the roots, through the xylem and out of the leaves is called the **transpiration stream**.

### Phloem

**Phloem** carries dissolved **sugars** made in photosynthesis from the leaves to the rest of the plant, for immediate use (respiration) or for storage (for example as starch in roots). This is called **translocation**.

- Phloem is made of living cells with sieve-like end walls (**sieve plates**), so cell sap can flow between them.
- Each sieve tube cell has a **companion cell** alongside it that provides energy.
- Translocation can go **both up and down** the plant, depending on where sugars are needed.

**Memory aid:** *Xylem* = *water*; *Phloem* = *food*.

activities.title: Worked example: comparing xylem and phloem
activities.content:
**Exam question style:** *Give two differences between xylem and phloem.*

The trick is to pair each point so the difference is clear:

| Feature | Xylem | Phloem |
|---|---|---|
| What it carries | Water and mineral ions | Dissolved sugars |
| Direction | Upwards only (roots to leaves) | Up and down (leaves to wherever needed) |
| Cells | Dead, hollow tubes | Living, with sieve plates and companion cells |
| Wall | Strengthened with lignin | No lignin |
| Process | Transpiration | Translocation |

A strong two-mark answer: *"Xylem carries water and minerals upwards in dead, lignified tubes, whereas phloem carries sugars in both directions through living sieve tubes."*

**Watch out:** many students say phloem carries "food". Be specific and write *dissolved sugars* (or sucrose) to get the mark.

question.text: Which statements are true of xylem? Select all that apply.
question.hint: Xylem is a pipe for water made of dead cells.
question.explanation: Xylem carries water and mineral ions upwards and its walls are strengthened with lignin. It is made of dead cells and it does not carry sugars, which is the job of phloem.

options.text: It transports water and mineral ions
Its walls are strengthened with lignin
It transports sugars from the leaves
It is made of living cells with companion cells

activities.title: Stomata and guard cells
activities.content:
## Pores that open and close

**Stomata** (singular: stoma) are tiny pores, mostly in the **lower epidermis** of a leaf. Each is surrounded by a pair of **guard cells** that change shape to open or close the pore.

- When the guard cells take in water they become swollen (turgid) and curve apart, **opening** the stoma.
- When they lose water they become limp (flaccid) and close the stoma.

Stomata are needed for **gas exchange**: carbon dioxide diffuses in for photosynthesis and oxygen diffuses out. But open stomata also let **water vapour** escape.

### Why are most stomata underneath?

The lower surface is shaded and cooler, so less water evaporates through it. Having most stomata there is a compromise: gases can still get in and out but water loss is reduced.

### Controlling water loss

In hot, dry conditions the guard cells lose water, so the stomata close. This protects the plant from wilting, though it also slows photosynthesis because less carbon dioxide can enter.

Stomata generally open in the light (when photosynthesis needs CO₂) and close in the dark.

question.text: Explain why having most stomata on the lower surface of a leaf helps a plant survive in dry weather.
question.hint: Compare the temperature of the upper and lower surfaces.
question.explanation: The lower surface is shaded and cooler than the upper surface, so less water evaporates from stomata there. This reduces water loss while still allowing gas exchange.

markScheme.criterion: Lower surface is cooler / shaded / not in direct sunlight
So less water evaporates / reduced water loss

activities.title: Transpiration and the factors that affect it
activities.content:
## What is transpiration?

**Transpiration** is the loss of water vapour from the leaves through the stomata. Water evaporates from the surfaces of the mesophyll cells into the air spaces, then diffuses out of the stomata. As water leaves the top of the plant, more is pulled up through the xylem from the roots. This continuous flow is the **transpiration stream**, and it delivers water and mineral ions to every part of the plant.

## Four factors that change the rate

| Factor | Effect on transpiration | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Temperature** | Increases with temperature | Water evaporates faster and molecules diffuse faster |
| **Humidity** | Decreases in humid air | Smaller difference in water vapour concentration between the leaf and the air, so diffusion is slower |
| **Air movement (wind)** | Increases with wind | Wind blows away the humid air around the stomata, keeping the concentration gradient steep |
| **Light intensity** | Increases in bright light | Stomata open wider for photosynthesis, so more water can escape |

The rate of transpiration can be measured with a **potometer**: a cut shoot is sealed to a tube of water and the distance a bubble moves along the tube in a set time shows how quickly water is taken up.

Rate = distance moved by bubble ÷ time.

activities.title: Worked example: potometer calculation
activities.content:
**A student sets up a potometer. In still air the bubble moves 24 mm in 10 minutes. With a fan blowing, it moves 60 mm in 10 minutes.**

**(a) Calculate the rate of water uptake in each condition.**

- Still air: 24 ÷ 10 = **2.4 mm/min**
- Fan: 60 ÷ 10 = **6.0 mm/min**

**(b) Explain the difference.**

The fan moves air across the leaves, removing the layer of humid air that builds up around the stomata. This keeps a large difference in water vapour concentration between the inside of the leaf and the air outside, so water vapour diffuses out faster. More water is lost, so more is drawn up through the xylem, and the bubble moves faster.

**(c) How many times faster was uptake with the fan?**

6.0 ÷ 2.4 = **2.5 times faster**.

**Fair test reminder:** everything else (temperature, light, the same shoot) must be kept constant so that air movement is the only variable changed.

question.text: In a potometer experiment, the air bubble moved 45 mm in 15 minutes. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm per minute.
A plant is moved from a dry room to a very humid greenhouse at the same temperature and light. What happens to its rate of transpiration and why?
question.hint: Diffusion depends on the difference in concentration between the leaf and the air.
question.explanation: In humid air there is more water vapour outside the leaf, so the concentration gradient is smaller and water vapour diffuses out more slowly. Transpiration decreases.

options.text: It decreases, because the concentration gradient of water vapour is smaller
It increases, because there is more water in the air to draw up
options.feedback: Plants take water from the soil, not the air.

options.text: It decreases, because the stomata are destroyed
It stays the same, because temperature is unchanged
options.feedback: Humidity affects transpiration independently of temperature.

metadata.blanksText: The movement of sugars through the phloem is called ___. The loss of water vapour from the leaves is called ___.

question.explanation: Sugar transport in phloem is translocation; water loss from leaves is transpiration.

question.text:
A gardener notices that the leaves of a plant wilt on a hot, windy afternoon but recover overnight.

(a) Explain why the plant loses water more quickly on a hot, windy afternoon. (2 marks)

(b) Describe how guard cells respond when the plant is short of water, and explain one disadvantage of this response for the plant. (2 marks)

(c) Name the tissue that replaces the lost water by carrying it up from the roots. (1 mark)
question.hint: For (a), give one reason for heat and one for wind. For (b), think about what happens to the supply of carbon dioxide.
question.explanation: (a) Higher temperature makes water evaporate and diffuse faster; wind removes humid air from around the stomata, maintaining a steep concentration gradient. (b) Guard cells lose water and become flaccid, closing the stomata; this reduces water loss but also stops carbon dioxide entering, so photosynthesis slows. (c) Xylem.

markScheme.criterion: Higher temperature increases evaporation / rate of diffusion
Wind removes water vapour from around the leaf, keeping a steep concentration gradient
Guard cells lose water / become flaccid and close the stomata
Disadvantage: less carbon dioxide enters so photosynthesis slows
Xylem named

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- Leaf tissues: **epidermis** (protective, waxy cuticle), **palisade mesophyll** (chloroplasts for photosynthesis), **spongy mesophyll** (air spaces), **xylem and phloem** in the veins, **stomata** in the lower epidermis.
- **Xylem**: dead, lignified tubes carrying water and minerals upwards (transpiration stream).
- **Phloem**: living sieve tubes with companion cells carrying dissolved sugars in both directions (translocation).
- **Stomata** are opened and closed by **guard cells**; most are on the cooler lower surface to limit water loss.
- **Transpiration** increases with temperature, light and wind, and decreases with humidity. Measure it with a potometer: rate = distance ÷ time.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: phloem transports water from the roots to the leaves.
practiceQuestions.hint: Remember the memory aid: xylem = water.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Water travels in the xylem. Phloem transports dissolved sugars.

options.text: True
False

practiceQuestions.text: Which leaf tissue contains the most chloroplasts?
practiceQuestions.hint: It is near the top where the light is strongest.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Palisade mesophyll cells are tightly packed near the upper surface and contain many chloroplasts.

options.text: Palisade mesophyll
Upper epidermis
options.feedback: The epidermis is transparent to let light through.

options.text: Xylem
Lower epidermis

metadata.blanksText: Xylem vessels are made of ___ cells and their walls are strengthened with ___.

practiceQuestions.hint: Xylem cells are not alive; the strengthening substance also makes wood hard.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Xylem is made of dead cells whose walls are strengthened with lignin.

practiceQuestions.text: Which conditions would increase the rate of transpiration? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about which conditions dry washing fastest.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Warm and windy conditions both speed up evaporation and diffusion of water vapour. High humidity and darkness (stomata closed) reduce transpiration.

options.text: Higher temperature
Stronger wind
Higher humidity
options.feedback: Humid air has a smaller concentration gradient, so transpiration slows.

options.text: Darkness
options.feedback: Stomata close in the dark, reducing water loss.

practiceQuestions.text: In a potometer, the bubble travelled 36 mm in 8 minutes. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm per minute.
practiceQuestions.hint: Divide the distance by the time.

practiceQuestions.text: Put these stages in order to describe the path of water through a plant.
practiceQuestions.hint: Start at the soil and end in the air.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Water enters root hair cells, travels up the xylem, evaporates from mesophyll cells into the air spaces, and diffuses out through the stomata.
order: Water is absorbed by root hair cells
Water travels up the stem in the xylem
Water evaporates from mesophyll cells into the air spaces
Water vapour diffuses out through the stomata

practiceQuestions.text: Describe how guard cells open a stoma.
practiceQuestions.hint: It involves water moving into the guard cells.
practiceQuestions.explanation: When guard cells absorb water they become turgid (swollen) and curve away from each other, which opens the pore between them.

markScheme.criterion: Guard cells take in / absorb water and become turgid or swollen
They change shape / curve apart so the pore opens

practiceQuestions.text: Match each process to its description.
practiceQuestions.hint: One is about water, one about sugar, one about gas.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Transpiration is water loss from leaves; translocation is movement of sugars in the phloem; gas exchange is the movement of CO₂ and O₂ through stomata.

pairs.right: Loss of water vapour from the leaves
Movement of dissolved sugars through the phloem
Movement of carbon dioxide and oxygen through the stomata

practiceQuestions.text:
A student compared two leaves of the same species. Leaf A grew in full sun; Leaf B grew in shade. Leaf A had a thicker waxy cuticle and more stomata per mm² than Leaf B.

(a) Explain how the thicker cuticle helps Leaf A. (1 mark)

(b) Suggest why Leaf A has more stomata per mm² than Leaf B. (1 mark)

(c) Explain **two** ways the structure of a leaf is adapted for efficient photosynthesis. (2 marks)
practiceQuestions.hint: In (b), think about how much carbon dioxide a leaf in bright light can use. In (c), consider surface area, thickness, chloroplasts or air spaces.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) A thicker waxy cuticle reduces water loss by evaporation, which matters in full sun. (b) In bright light photosynthesis is faster, so more stomata allow more carbon dioxide to diffuse in. (c) Any two: a broad shape gives a large surface area to absorb light; the leaf is thin so gases have a short diffusion distance; palisade cells are packed with chloroplasts; air spaces in the spongy mesophyll let gases diffuse to cells.

markScheme.criterion: Thicker cuticle reduces water loss / evaporation
More stomata allow more carbon dioxide in for faster photosynthesis in bright light
First adaptation with reason (e.g. large surface area for light, thin for short diffusion distance)
Second, different adaptation with reason

practiceQuestions.text: Which of these is the correct role of companion cells?
practiceQuestions.hint: They sit next to phloem sieve tubes.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Companion cells sit alongside phloem sieve tube cells and provide the energy needed for translocation.

options.text: They provide energy for the phloem sieve tubes
They strengthen xylem with lignin
They open and close stomata
options.feedback: That is the job of guard cells.

options.text: They absorb water from the soil

practiceQuestions.text: Match each plant tissue to its function.
practiceQuestions.hint: Two are transport tissues, one makes new cells and one is a protective covering.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Xylem carries water and mineral ions up from the roots; phloem carries dissolved sugars; meristem tissue at the root and shoot tips divides to make new cells; epidermal tissue covers and protects the plant's surfaces.

pairs.right: Transports water and mineral ions up from the roots
Transports dissolved sugars around the plant
Divides to produce new cells at root and shoot tips
Covers and protects the surface of the plant

practiceQuestions.text: Which statements are true of phloem? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Phloem is the living transport tissue for the products of photosynthesis.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Phloem is made of living cells (sieve tubes with companion cells) and carries dissolved sugars both up and down the plant. Lignin-strengthened walls and water transport from the roots are features of xylem.

options.text: It transports dissolved sugars both up and down the plant
It is made of living cells
Its walls are strengthened with lignin
It carries water up from the roots

practiceQuestions.text: Explain why a thick waxy cuticle on the upper surface of its leaves helps a plant survive in a hot, sunny climate.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what the cuticle stops, and why the upper surface in particular needs that protection.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The waxy cuticle is waterproof, so it stops water evaporating through the epidermis and reduces water loss. The upper surface faces direct sunlight and is the hottest part of the leaf, so without the cuticle evaporation there would be greatest.

markScheme.criterion: Waxy cuticle is waterproof, so it reduces evaporation / water loss from the leaf surface
Upper surface is in direct sunlight / hottest, so evaporation would otherwise be fastest there

practiceQuestions.text: A student sets up a potometer with a leafy laurel shoot. Once the shoot has settled, the air bubble travels 56 mm in 16 minutes. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm per minute.
practiceQuestions.hint: Divide the distance moved by the time taken.

practiceQuestions.text: A potted plant is moved from a room with still air to a spot in front of a fan. Temperature, light and humidity are kept the same. What happens to its rate of transpiration and why?
practiceQuestions.hint: Water vapour that leaves the stomata normally builds up in a thin layer around the leaf.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Moving air sweeps away the humid layer of water vapour that builds up around the leaf, so the concentration gradient between the inside of the leaf and the air stays steep and water vapour diffuses out faster. Transpiration increases.

options.text: It increases, because moving air removes water vapour from around the leaf and keeps the concentration gradient steep
It decreases, because the wind pushes the stomata shut
options.feedback: Stomata close in response to water shortage, not to air movement.

options.text: It stays the same, because the temperature has not changed
options.feedback: Air movement affects transpiration independently of temperature.

options.text: It increases, because the wind pushes water up the xylem

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the sentences about plant tissues and structures.

metadata.blanksText: The tissue at the tips of roots and shoots that keeps dividing to produce new cells is called ___ tissue. The tiny pores in the lower epidermis that let gases in and out are called ___.

practiceQuestions.hint: The first is where plant growth happens; the second word is the plural of stoma.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Meristem tissue contains cells that divide to produce new plant cells. Stomata are the pores in the epidermis through which gases and water vapour pass.

practiceQuestions.text:
A student uses a potometer to measure the water uptake of a leafy shoot under three conditions:

- Condition 1: 15 °C, still air
- Condition 2: 25 °C, still air
- Condition 3: 25 °C, with a fan blowing across the leaves

Water uptake was lowest in condition 1 and highest in condition 3.

(a) Explain why water uptake was higher in condition 2 than in condition 1. (2 marks)

(b) Explain why water uptake was higher in condition 3 than in condition 2. (1 mark)

(c) The student then smeared petroleum jelly over the lower surface of every leaf and repeated condition 3. Water uptake fell sharply. Explain why. (2 marks)
practiceQuestions.hint: For (a), think about the energy of water molecules. For (c), think about where most stomata are and what the jelly does to them.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) At the higher temperature the water molecules have more energy, so water evaporates from the cells inside the leaf faster and water vapour diffuses out through the stomata more quickly; the shoot takes up more water to replace what is lost. (b) The fan removes the humid air from around the leaves, keeping a steep concentration gradient of water vapour, so diffusion out of the leaf is faster. (c) Most stomata are on the lower surface of the leaf; the jelly blocks these pores, so water vapour cannot escape and transpiration falls, so much less water is taken up.

markScheme.criterion: Higher temperature gives water molecules more energy so evaporation is faster
Water vapour diffuses out through the stomata faster, so more water is taken up to replace it
Fan / moving air removes water vapour from around the leaf, keeping a steep concentration gradient
Petroleum jelly blocks / covers the stomata
Most stomata are on the lower surface, so water vapour cannot escape and transpiration falls
